doc_summary: A Redwood post on adapting control evaluations into safety cases for real deployments, covering how to build proxy environments, keep red teams competitive, and estimate risk cheaply and conservatively. It repeatedly addresses indistinguishability of synthetic/proxy inputs from reality and models evaluation-aware behaviour (e.g. vigilant humans, blue team discriminating eval vs deployment).

items.claim: In a setup, make eval inputs and tasks hard to distinguish from reality (and mix real and eval tasks freely) instead of letting participants know they are being evaluated, because otherwise behaviour in the eval (e.g. vigilance) won't match deployment.
items.quote: Make evaluations hard to distinguish from reality from the perspective of human labor. This seems difficult and poses various issues with proxy bad outcomes, but if it was hard to distinguish and we mixed real and evaluation tasks freely, then our evaluations would be faithful.

items.claim: Prefers measuring synthetic-input realism as a discrimination gap between proxy and real inputs over assuming synthetic inputs are realistic, because a differential degradation in realism between proxy and reality is what makes the eval inaccurate.
items.quote: Now, we’ll train a model to discriminate between proxy input and the corresponding synthetic inputs and train a model to discriminate between real inputs and the corresponding synthetic inputs. If the discrimination profile is very similar, then there is no problem.

items.claim: Distrusts proxy environments that are especially good at constructing the specific rare inputs of interest (e.g. takeover opportunities), since realism can fail differentially exactly where the test matters most, even if the general distribution looks fine.
items.quote: If our synthetic input process is basically equally good at constructing synthetic inputs for the general distribution for both reality and the proxy environment, but the generation process is much better at the specific inputs we’re interested in for the proxy environment than for reality, our evaluation could be inaccurate.

items.claim: Distrusts evaluation results where the protocol/blue team can tell eval from deployment, because it can behave differently (cheat) when it detects which is being measured.
items.quote: Then, the blue team could cheat by having the protocol discriminate whether or not usefulness or safety is currently being measured and apply less stringent countermeasures if usefulness is being measured.

items.claim: Worries that AI-recognisable 'far-from-human' behaviours let models distinguish synthetic test examples from genuine attempts, defeating honeypot-style checks.
items.quote: far-from-human approaches might be problematic even if they aren’t more directly effective than the best red team approaches because they might enable AIs to discriminate synthetic examples of AI takeover attempts we create from actual actions taken by an AI trying to take over.

items.claim: In a setup, keep realism by having the adversarial model's trigger/classifier use only what a real model would have (a single forward pass), instead of granting extra reasoning or unrealistic knowledge, because unrealistic allowances make the test uninformative.
items.quote: This classifier should only allow for a single forward pass (or whatever uninterpretable reasoning is available) to ensure realism.

items.claim: Prefers proxy bad outcomes that are benign but share the core difficulty (capture-the-flag style) over real catastrophic objectives, because they are safe to run and cleanly checkable.
items.quote: we can use proxy bad outcomes that share some of the same core difficulties but would likely be benign if an AI escaped from the lab. This is similar to “capture the flag” cybersecurity contests

items.claim: In a setup, use the actual deployment infrastructure and exact models as much as possible instead of extrapolating from weaker models or toy stand-ins, because this makes the safety estimate more accurate.
items.quote: a red team executes modified versions of parts of the actual attack while using as much of the real infrastructure as possible in order to make the estimate of safety as accurate as possible.

items.claim: Give the model a analogous stand-in for knowledge it plausibly has but is hard to elicit (e.g. describe an analogous vulnerability in the prompt) so the scenario tests the behaviour without needing the real thing.
items.quote: if we think it’s likely that AIs know about a zero-day vulnerability in linux (based on pretraining), then we could set up a proxy environment where we describe analogous vulnerabilities in the prompt, and see if AIs can be trained to successfully exploit vulnerabilities.

items.claim: Prefers legibly convincing evidence over borderline evidence for high-stakes claims like 'AI is catastrophically misaligned', because a single false positive is extremely costly.
items.quote: by forcing the auditing process to only declare an AI catastrophically misaligned if the evidence is very legibly convincing.

items.claim: Prefers conservative, adversarially-minimised safety estimates (worst case across attack strategies, red team incentivised to win) over average-case results, because the opponent is a potentially scheming model.
items.quote: Since we are in an adversarial situation against a potentially malicious AI, the safety of a protocol is the minimum safety across all attack strategies suggested by the red team.
